sentences.text: The species name lucivenator combines Latin words for 'light' and 'hunter'.
A notable feature is a rostral boss, an expanded skull structure stretching along the dorsal surface just before the eyes.
The second posterior knob on the maxilla is described as more pronounced than the midrostral boss.
The skull table is trapezoidal and primarily formed by the frontal, parietal, postorbital, and squamosal bones.
The postorbital bones form pronounced squamosal horns that are most developed in the largest specimens.
Brochu and colleagues formally named this species in 2026.
Fossils were found in Ethiopia at the type locality known as the Hadar Formation.
The holotype, the specimen the species is based on, is cataloged as A.L. 138-16 and includes a complete cranium with a matching lower jaw.
Remains occur in three of the four members of the Hadar Formation: Sidi Hakoma, Denen Dora, and Kada Hadar.
The largest individuals reached lengths of 4 to 5 meters and weights of 300 to 600 kilograms.
One specimen preserves five furrows and a puncture wound on its lower jaw.
Healing bone texture suggests the crocodile survived the injury and lived for a significant time after the encounter.
Evidence indicates the wounds were caused by another crocodile rather than a mammal.
The injury patterns suggest the crocodile used feeding maneuvers like the death roll or head thrashing during an attack.
This extinct crocodile belongs to the genus Crocodylus with the specific epithet lucivenator.
It appears to be closely related to Paleoafrican Crocodylus species from East Africa rather than modern African crocodiles.
It belongs to the Palaeoafrican Crocodylus clade, which is distantly related to modern Neoafrican crocodiles like the Nile and Sacred crocodiles.
Crocodylus lucivenator lived during the Pliocene epoch as an extinct crocodile from the Late Pliocene Hadar Formation in Ethiopia.
The Hadar Formation environment consisted of mixed woodlands and grasslands with large paleolakes at certain times.
It is debated whether the Palaeoafrican group including Crocodylus lucivenator should clade with modern Neotropic Crocodylus, as alternative phylogenetic results are possible.
